subsystems.name: Absorber ensemble
subsystems.role: the storage medium — a set of identical quantum units (dye molecules, trapped atoms, or superconducting qubits) whose excited states hold the energy.
parts: molecules or qubits with a chosen transition frequency
uniform transition energies across the ensemble

subsystems.name: Shared electromagnetic mode
subsystems.role: a single cavity or resonator field that every absorber couples to, so they act collectively rather than independently.
parts: high quality-factor mirrors or superconducting cavity walls

subsystems.name: Coupling and tuning stage
subsystems.role: keeps all absorbers within the collective linewidth and aligned to the same field, which is what produces the superlinear (Dickie-type) charging rate.

subsystems.name: Coherence protection
subsystems.role: slows dephasing so the collective effect survives long enough to charge and discharge.

subsystems.name: Extraction and output stage
subsystems.role: the missing piece: a switch or transducer that moves stored energy into a useful load without destroying the coherence that produced the fast charge.
parts: load circuit, transducer or optical output

subsystems.name: Control and readout
subsystems.role: measures how much energy is stored and how the charge rate scales with the number of absorbers.

buildSteps.title: Pick the platform
buildSteps.detail: Choose between molecular absorbers in an optical microcavity (cheap, room temperature) or superconducting qubits in a microwave resonator (fast, controllable, but needs millikelvin cooling). Each gives up something the other has.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the resonator
buildSteps.detail: Mirror stacks for an optical cavity, or lithographically patterned superconducting metal on silicon for a microwave one, tuned so the mode frequency matches the absorbers.

buildSteps.title: Place the absorbers
buildSteps.detail: Molecules are embedded in a host film or self-assembled layer; qubits are patterned directly. Spacing and dipole orientation are controlled so all units see the same field strength.

buildSteps.title: Couple them collectively
buildSteps.detail: Trim each absorber onto resonance and verify that the charge rate grows faster than linearly with the number of units — the signature of collective charging.

buildSteps.title: Isolate from the environment
buildSteps.detail: Cool and shield the device to push coherence times well beyond the charging time; this is where molecular systems and qubits currently diverge sharply in performance.

buildSteps.title: Add the charging pump
buildSteps.detail: Deliver energy into the shared mode with a pulse, laser or microwave drive, timed to the collective dynamics rather than to individual absorbers.

buildSteps.title: Open an extraction path
buildSteps.detail: Insert a controllable switch between the storage ensemble and a load. Discharging must be fast and must not scramble the state, which is the tightest known constraint on the whole idea.

buildSteps.title: Measure round-trip efficiency
buildSteps.detail: Record energy out divided by energy in, charge rate versus absorber count, and coherence time. A useful device needs all three measured on the same apparatus.

buildSteps.title: Scale the ensemble
buildSteps.detail: Increase the number of absorbers while preserving the superlinear scaling. Decoherence and fabrication spread grow with size, so the advantage may not survive to useful capacities.

prerequisites.why: collective effects need the absorbers to stay in step; today's best qubits and molecular systems hold coherence for orders of magnitude less than a practical charge–discharge cycle would need.
single-emitter cavity coupling is routine, but coupling many identical emitters to one mode without inhomogeneous broadening spoiling the collective rate is not solved.
no demonstrated method moves stored quantum energy into an electrical or mechanical load efficiently while preserving the coherence that enabled fast charging.
measuring stored energy without disturbing it, and switching the device on demand, requires control electronics close to today's state of the art.
absorbers must be near-identical in frequency to within the collective linewidth across a large ensemble — a yield problem, not just a physics one.

pathway.milestone: small-scale demonstrations of superlinear charging and superabsorption in molecular and microwave-cavity systems
pathway.unlocks: confidence that the collective effect is real and can be measured, plus theoretical limits on how much it can help.

pathway.milestone: a laboratory device that charges fast, stores a measurable amount of energy and discharges it to a load with published round-trip efficiency
pathway.unlocks: the first honest comparison against a supercapacitor or lithium-ion cell — noting that quantum batteries offer a rate advantage, not a capacity advantage.

pathway.milestone: hybrid architectures where a quantum charging stage tops up a conventional cell on a chip
pathway.unlocks: niche uses such as ultrafast pulsed power in microelectronics, where charge speed matters more than energy density.

pathway.milestone: large coherent ensembles with engineered extraction interfaces
pathway.unlocks: either a genuine new storage class for short bursts of power, or a clear result that decoherence makes the advantage unattainable — both are useful outcomes.
nothing yet; quantum batteries are unlikely to compete with existing storage on cost per kilowatt-hour, since their proposed benefit is charging speed.
